title: AI in Project Management
sequence: Introduction (an emerging trend that touches all later topics).

header.html: New in 2026: AI was added to the exam through PMI's job task analysis and appears as a theme across domains rather than as its own task. Exam situations include using AI to analyze data and forecast, drafting artifacts, handling AI output that conflicts with team judgment, and the ethical, security and privacy responsibilities of using it. Related enablers: collect and analyze data to make informed project decisions (Process Task 1), reporting and communication (People Task 8, Process Task 9), risk (Business Environment Task 5), compliance (Business Environment Task 2).

Appendix X3 (X3.1 AI in the project context and adoption strategies, X3.2 common use cases, X3.3 responsible use and ethical concerns); Section 5 tools (AI/ML/NLP, predictive analytics, process automation, genetic algorithms, AR/VR); AI passages in Governance (knowledge), Stakeholders, Risk, Resources and Appendix X4 (contracts)

html:
1What AI Is (Terms)

Term PMBOK 8 meaning
Artificial intelligence (AI) Technologies that simulate human behavior on computers: systems that can reason, learn and act autonomously; machines that can perform tasks they were not directly programmed for, learn from experience and adapt
Machine learning (ML) Subfield of AI that uses data to train models that predict outputs from previous inputs
Deep learning (DL) More advanced ML using multilayered neural networks; needs large data sets and much computing
Generative AI (GenAI) Subset of deep learning that applies large language models (LLMs) to generate new text, speech, audio, pictures and video; GPT is an example
Natural language processing (NLP) Software that processes natural language: chatbots, speech recognition, text extraction and summarization, sentiment analysis
Predictive analytics ML on current and historical data to find patterns and forecast performance, trends, events and risks
Process automation / RPA Rule-based software robots that mimic human actions for repeatable tasks (scheduling meetings, reminders)
Genetic algorithms An optimization technique inspired by natural selection; can explore many decision combinations without human bias, e.g., scheduling, resource leveling, critical path planning
AR / VR Augmented reality overlays digital information on the physical world; virtual reality is an interactive 3D simulated environment

Why it matters: AI can shift project work from repetitive tasks to higher-level, creative and strategic work, supporting decisions, automating routine work and improving forecasting. The Standard says project managers should be skilled strategists and change managers, with AI helping them focus on strategy, stakeholder engagement, innovation and improvement. The impact of AI depends on the quality of its inputs and on human oversight.

2Adoption Strategies: Automation, Assistance, Augmentation

Classify tasks by complexity and the need for human supervision; the more complex the task, the more human intervention is required for a high-quality result.

Strategy Task profile PMBOK 8 examples Human role
Automation Low complexity, little human intervention in the final output Report generation, document analysis, conference-call summarization; reuse standard prompts across projects and teams (e.g., a prompt library) Sets rules, spot-checks
Assistance Tool complements analysis and builds ideas iteratively toward an expected output Creating a risk register or a scheduling plan with buffers First iterations are not complete; a professional reviews for accuracy and completeness
Augmentation Enhances existing capabilities and explores new ones on strategic, complex tasks Balancing a project portfolio to maximize ROI; risk forecasting with external variables Use the tool as a brainstorming partner, exchanging and refining ideas through multiple iterations

State of the market: many tools are free or paid. Free ones usually limit prompts per period; the big difference is how the tool treats user data. Paid versions can restrict the use of your data to retrain models, protecting privacy and intellectual property.

3Use Cases by Performance Domain (Table X3-1)

Domain Use case (strategy)
Governance Data-driven decision-making for project selection (augmentation); multicriteria decision analysis (assistance); brainstorming and idea generation, including drafts of business cases and charters (augmentation); AI-enhanced collaboration platforms (assistance); automated reporting and dashboards (automation); process automation of documentation, reports, compliance checks (automation); predictive analytics for planning (assistance); real-time monitoring against baselines (automation); early-warning signals from pattern recognition (assistance); baseline optimization across scope, schedule, cost (augmentation); AI chatbots (automation); task management (automation); automated meeting minutes and summaries (automation)
Risk Risk identification and assessment from historical data and benchmarks (augmentation); automated mitigation actions from rules (automation); risk impact analysis (assistance); risk-adjusted ROI analysis (augmentation)
Stakeholders Stakeholder sentiment analysis with NLP, used ethically (augmentation); personalized communication based on preferences (augmentation)
Schedule Dynamic scheduling (assistance); schedule conflict resolution (assistance); schedule risk impact analysis (assistance)

Elsewhere in the Guide

  • Stakeholders: AI-powered tools help collect, analyze and present data so stakeholders decide faster and with more confidence; decide per project where AI assists (e.g., producing communication artifacts); apply security and ethics measures and involve the cybersecurity team to judge whether the risk is acceptable.
  • Knowledge management: AI (e.g., interview bots) helps capture tacit and explicit knowledge and is a major source of knowledge, but it carries risks: unintentionally exposing sensitive information and AI hallucinations. Projects should have responsible AI policies to manage related knowledge.
  • Risk: GenAI and data analytics complement risk identification and analysis.
  • Procurement: AI-powered contract analysis for risk assessment, faster negotiation, compliance monitoring and cost-overrun prediction (Topic 22).
  • Resources / technology impact (Standard): AI and ML offer predictive insights on resources and risks; the team must ensure data accuracy and neutral outputs (avoid bias) and align with IT to safeguard information.
  • Communication skills: writing AI prompts is now part of electronic communication skills.

4Responsible Use and Ethical Concerns

Concern What PMBOK 8 says
Bias AI can be biased if trained on biased data or built with biased algorithms. Mitigate by diversifying training data, testing periodically (focused on bias), and involving different teams in development
Privacy AI uses large, sensitive data sets regulated by privacy policies and laws; secure the data and collect it under a privacy policy; risk of violating privacy or ethical standards
Accountability A human must be accountable for each decision, with accountability clearly defined
Reliability Information from AI should be checked and validated; it may be biased, incorrect or irrelevant
Safety Design, test and monitor to the required safety level
Transparency Share with users and affected parties how data is used and handled, how algorithms work and how decisions are made
Copyright Ownership of AI-generated content is a dilemma; know regulations and laws on the data used; consider the level of human contribution
Sustainability Each AI request consumes electricity, water and other resources; weigh this when deciding where to use AI
  • Organizational ethical guidelines and AI policies are the foundation for a common understanding of acceptable use. Project professionals should foster a culture of awareness and ethical use and take responsibility within the team for ethical AI decisions.
  • It is up to humans to take the risks into account and decide on AI's use. This aligns with the PMI Code of Ethics (responsibility, honesty, fairness; Topic 06).

5How the Project Manager Uses AI Well

Beyond PMBOK 8exam practice

  1. Decide where AI helps (routine drafting, data analysis, forecasting) and where human judgment must lead (stakeholder relationships, ethics, trade-offs, accountability).
  2. Check policy first: organizational AI policy, approved tools, data classification; involve cybersecurity, legal and data protection when needed.
  3. Protect data: never paste confidential, personal or contractual data into unapproved or public tools.
  4. Validate outputs against data and SMEs; correct hallucinations before use or distribution (minutes, reports, risk registers, estimates).
  5. Treat AI forecasts as inputs, not verdicts. When an AI forecast conflicts with the team's view, investigate the data and assumptions, discuss with the team, and decide; do not blindly follow or dismiss either.
  6. Be transparent with stakeholders about AI use where it affects them; do not use AI to monitor people unethically.
  7. Keep humans accountable and document decisions.
  8. Build skills: prompt writing, data literacy, bias awareness; reuse good prompts.

6Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Planning and estimates Predictive analytics on historical data, baseline optimization, schedule conflict resolution Backlog drafting, story refinement, velocity-based forecasting, release planning support Both
Monitoring Automated reporting, early-warning signals against baselines Dashboards, burn charts and flow metrics with anomaly alerts Unified dashboard
Team collaboration Meeting minutes, task reminders Retrospective summaries, interview bots for knowledge Both
Risk AI-assisted risk register and impact analysis Risk-adjusted backlog suggestions each iteration Both
Caution Do not let a forecast replace baseline governance Do not replace team conversation with bot summaries Keep one accountable human view

7Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. A human stays accountable. AI recommends; the PM and organization decide and own the outcome.
  2. Validate before you trust. Check AI output for errors, bias and irrelevance (hallucinations) before it goes into reports, registers, minutes or decisions.
  3. Protect sensitive data. Do not use public AI tools for confidential or personal information; follow organizational policy and use approved tools.
  4. Policy and cybersecurity come first when adopting a new tool; assess risk acceptability with the right stakeholders.
  5. Match the AI strategy to the task: automate routine work, use AI to assist analysis (with review), and augment complex strategic work with human judgment.
  6. AI conflicts with team judgment: investigate and reconcile; neither obey nor ignore.
  7. Bias and fairness: diversify data, test for bias, involve different teams; do not apply biased tools to people decisions.
  8. Transparency and copyright: tell affected parties how AI is used; know the legal position on generated content.
  9. Ethical use of sentiment analysis: use it to understand and engage stakeholders, respecting privacy; not for surveillance or manipulation.
  10. AI does not replace leadership: combine AI with leadership, communication and stakeholder engagement.

8Exam Q&A

8.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1An AI forecasting tool predicts that the release will slip by three weeks, but the scrum team believes its sprint plan is sound. What should the project manager do?

  • AReview the tool's data and assumptions with the team before deciding
  • BAsk the tool vendor to adjust the forecast to match the team's view
  • CDisregard the forecast because the team knows the work much better
  • DAccept the forecast as it stands and replan the schedule immediately
Show the answer

Answer: A. AI output is an input to be validated, so the project manager reconciles it with the team's analysis and actual progress before deciding. Obeying it, dismissing it or asking the vendor to change it each skips that validation.

S2A project manager pasted a client's confidential contract terms into a free public AI chatbot to draft a summary. What should she do now?

  • ADelete the conversation and keep the incident entirely to herself
  • BStop, report the exposure under policy and use only approved tools
  • CAsk colleagues to use the same chatbot to share the time savings
  • DContinue using the chatbot, since the summary is accurate and useful
Show the answer

Answer: B. Confidential data must be protected under privacy and security policy, so she stops, owns the mistake and reports the exposure. Continuing, hiding it or spreading the practice makes the breach worse.

S3The team spends hours each week compiling routine status reports from tracking data. Which AI adoption strategy fits best?

  • AAutomation of report generation, with a review before distribution
  • BAugmentation, with several rounds of human iteration on every report
  • CNo AI use at all, because status reports are strategic documents
  • DReplace the stakeholder meetings with the automated reports entirely
Show the answer

Answer: A. Low-complexity, repeatable tasks suit automation, with a human check before reports are issued. Heavy iteration is for strategic tasks, and reports do not replace stakeholder conversations.

S4An AI tool produces a draft risk register for an agile project in minutes. What should the project manager do?

  • APublish it as the final risk register without further changes
  • BReview and refine it with the team and subject matter experts
  • CReplace the team's risk workshops with the AI output from now on
  • DDiscard the draft because the team's own judgment is more reliable
Show the answer

Answer: B. Drafting a risk register is an assistance use: the first output is not complete, so a professional reviews it for accuracy and completeness with the team. Publishing it, discarding it or replacing the workshops misuses the tool.

S5An AI sentiment tool flags a key stakeholder as increasingly negative based on analysis of emails. What is the best use of this information?

  • AShare the analysis widely so that the team can adapt its tone
  • BDisregard the flag because AI cannot judge human feelings reliably from emails
  • CTreat it as a signal and meet the stakeholder to understand concerns
  • DEscalate the stakeholder to the sponsor as a project problem
Show the answer

Answer: C. Sentiment analysis supports engagement when used ethically: it is a signal to confirm directly with the stakeholder while respecting privacy policies. Escalating, ignoring or broadcasting it does not engage the person.

S6An AI resource-allocation tool consistently recommends assignments that favor one group of team members. What should the project manager do?

  • AKeep the pattern quiet so that team morale is not affected at all
  • BFollow the recommendations because the tool is purely data-driven
  • CStop using any planning tool and assign the work at random instead
  • DInvestigate bias in the data and algorithm and keep human review
Show the answer

Answer: D. Bias is mitigated by testing the tool, diversifying data, involving different teams and keeping human review of assignments. Blind trust, random assignment or hiding the pattern leaves the unfairness in place.

S7An AI notetaker's minutes of a sprint review record a decision that was not actually made. What should the project manager do?

  • AValidate the minutes with the attendees and correct them before issue
  • BAdd a note that the minutes are provisional and issue them anyway
  • CDelete the minutes and ask everyone to rely on their own memory
  • DDistribute the minutes as they are, since the tool recorded them
Show the answer

Answer: A. The reliability of AI output must be checked, and humans remain accountable for records, so the minutes are validated with the attendees and corrected before issue. Issuing them, discarding them or labeling them provisional lets an error stand.

S8A product team wants to start using an AI tool to analyze user stories, but the organization has no AI policy. What should the project manager do first?

  • ABan the use of all AI tools on the project until a formal policy exists
  • BEngage governance, cybersecurity and legal to define acceptable use
  • CLet the team use the tool informally and review the results later
  • DBuy the most capable commercial tool and rely on its safeguards
Show the answer

Answer: B. Before adoption, acceptability must be assessed and rules defined with governance, cybersecurity and legal, as PMBOK 8 advises for AI use. Informal use, a blanket ban or reliance on a vendor's safeguards skips that assessment.

S9A team used generative AI to produce part of a deliverable, and the customer now asks about its ownership and origin. What should the project manager do?

  • ARemove the AI-generated content silently before the next release
  • BState that the content is entirely the original work of the team
  • CBe transparent about the AI use and check the legal and licensing position
  • DRefuse to answer until the customer signs a confidentiality agreement
Show the answer

Answer: C. Transparency and copyright awareness apply to AI-generated content: the use is disclosed, the legal position is checked and the level of human contribution is documented. Claiming originality, refusing or removing it silently is not transparent.

S10A lessons learned entry captured by an AI interview bot after a release contains a claim that nobody can verify. What should the project manager do?

  • AApply it in the next project plan as a proven working assumption
  • BAdd it to the repository as captured, since the bot recorded it
  • CDelete every lesson that the AI interview bot has produced so far in this project
  • DVerify it with the people involved before it enters the repository
Show the answer

Answer: D. AI hallucinations and unverifiable content must be validated before they become organizational knowledge. Adding, applying or wholesale deleting the bot's output skips the validation that makes lessons trustworthy.

8.2 Recall Q&As

R1What is the relationship between AI, ML, DL and GenAI?

Show the answer

ML is a subfield of AI, deep learning is an advanced type of ML, and generative AI is a subset of deep learning using large language models.

R2Name the three AI adoption strategies.

Show the answer

Automation, assistance, augmentation.

R3Give an example of each.

Show the answer

Automation: report generation or call summaries; assistance: drafting a risk register or schedule with buffers; augmentation: portfolio balancing for ROI or risk forecasting with external variables.

R4What must a professional do with first AI iterations?

Show the answer

Review them for accuracy and completeness; they are not complete.

R5Which ethical concerns does PMBOK 8 name for AI?

Show the answer

Bias, privacy, accountability, reliability, safety, transparency, copyright, sustainability.

R6How can bias be mitigated?

Show the answer

Diversify training data, test periodically with a focus on bias, involve different teams in development.

R7Why might a paid AI tool be preferable?

Show the answer

Paid versions can restrict the use of your data to retrain models, protecting privacy and intellectual property.

R8What risks come with AI in knowledge management?

Show the answer

Unintentionally exposing sensitive information and AI hallucinations; projects need responsible AI policies.

R9Who is accountable for decisions informed by AI?

Show the answer

A human; accountability should be clearly defined.

R10What is NLP and one use in stakeholder work?

Show the answer

Natural language processing processes human language; stakeholder sentiment analysis of communications.

R11What is predictive analytics?

Show the answer

ML on current and historical data to predict future scenarios, performance and risks.

R12What resource does each AI request consume that should be considered?

Show the answer

Electricity, water and other resources (sustainability concern).

9Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
AI hierarchy AI > ML > DL > GenAI (LLMs); NLP; predictive analytics
Strategies Automation (routine) · Assistance (review needed) · Augmentation (strategic, human + AI iterate)
Use cases Reporting, monitoring, minutes, risk drafts, scheduling optimization, sentiment analysis, personalized communication
Ethics Bias · privacy · accountability · reliability · safety · transparency · copyright · sustainability
Bias fix Diverse data, periodic tests, diverse teams
Accountability Always a human
Data Never put confidential or personal data in public tools; paid tools can limit training use
Knowledge risk Exposed sensitive data and hallucinations; responsible AI policy
Adoption Policy, cybersecurity, legal first; decide per project
First-action pattern Check policy, protect data, validate the output, keep a human accountable, be transparent
